**How the blocks are picked.** `get_matching_blocks` is a divide-and-conquer around `find_longest_match`. It finds the single longest contiguous run shared by `a[alo:ahi]` and `b[blo:bhi]`, records it, then repeats on the piece to the left of that run and the piece to the right (using an explicit queue rather than recursion). At the end it sorts the blocks, merges any that turned out adjacent, and appends the `(len(a), len(b), 0)` sentinel. Because each match is fixed before its neighbours are considered, the result is not a minimal edit script or a true longest common subsequence. It is greedy by "biggest contiguous chunk first", which is what makes the diffs look natural to people.

**How one longest match is found.** `__chain_b` precomputes `b2j`, a map from each element of `b` to the list of positions where it occurs. `find_longest_match` then walks `a` one element at a time, keeping `j2len[j]`, the length of the match ending at `a[i-1]` and `b[j]`. For each occurrence `j` of `a[i]` in `b`, the new length is `j2len[j-1] + 1`. The best is only replaced on a strictly greater length, so ties go to the block starting earliest in `a`, then earliest in `b`.

**What junk does.** If you pass `isjunk`, every element of `b` it flags is deleted from `b2j` (and remembered in `bjunk`). The practical consequences are:

- **Junk cannot seed a match.** The inner loop never sees a junk element, so the core match is entirely junk-free.
- **Junk can still be absorbed at the edges.** After the core match is found, it is extended outward over matching non-junk elements, then over matching junk elements. So junk ends up inside a block only when it sits next to a real match.
- **Junk-only regions mostly don't match.** If a sub-range has nothing interesting in common, the core match is empty at `(alo, blo)`, and only identical elements at the very start of both ranges can be picked up by the extension.
- **It is asymmetric.** Junk is only evaluated on `b`, so swapping `a` and `b` can give different blocks.

The point is to stop the algorithm from anchoring on blanks or whitespace. The `private volatile Thread currentThread;` comment in the source is the motivating case.

**What autojunk does.** When `autojunk=True` and `len(b) >= 200`, any non-junk element occurring more than `len(b)//100 + 1` times in `b` is also removed from `b2j` and recorded in `bpopular`. These "popular" elements behave like junk in that they cannot seed a match, but they are not in `bjunk`, so they are picked up in the first (non-junk) extension pass. This is mainly a speed heuristic: the inner loop's cost is driven by how many times each element occurs in `b`, so dropping lines like `return NULL;` or blank lines removes most of the quadratic work.

**The effect on results.** For line-level diffs, autojunk usually costs little: popular lines still get matched when they adjoin a distinctive line, and you get at worst a slightly less tight diff. Note that `unified_diff` and `context_diff` pass `isjunk=None` but leave autojunk on. The damage shows up when the alphabet is small relative to the length, such as comparing strings of 200+ characters character by character. There nearly every character is popular, `b2j` is nearly empty, and few or no matches can be seeded. Matching blocks are then missed and `ratio()` (which is `2*M/T` over the matched total) can come out far lower than the sequences' real similarity. Passing `autojunk=False` fixes that, at the cost of the worst-case quadratic time.

**What the loop computes.** The loop is Euclid's algorithm run on `n/d`, which produces the continued-fraction expansion of the fraction one term `a` at a time. Alongside it, the loop maintains the last two *convergents*, `p0/q0` and `p1/q1`, using the standard recurrence `p_new = p0 + a*p1`, `q_new = q0 + a*q1`. Convergents alternate above and below the true value and their denominators grow, so the loop stops as soon as the next convergent's denominator `q2` would exceed `max_denominator`. Because the early return has already handled `self._denominator <= max_denominator`, that break always happens before `d` reaches zero.

**Why that gives the right answer.** The theorem cited in the comment says the best one-sided approximations to `x` are exactly the convergents and the *semiconvergents*: fractions `(p0 + k*p1)/(q0 + k*q1)` for `k` between 0 and the next term `a`. At the break there are only two candidates left:

- **`p1/q1`**: the last convergent that fits, lying on one side of `x`.
- **`(p0 + k*p1)/(q0 + k*q1)`** with `k = (max_denominator - q0)//q1`: the furthest semiconvergent that still fits, lying on the other side of `x`.

These are the best lower and best upper approximations within the denominator limit, so the closest fraction overall must be one of them.

**How it picks between the two.** The final `if` compares them without building any fractions:

- The two candidates are exactly `1/(q1*(q0+k*q1))` apart, because adjacent convergents satisfy `p0*q1 - p1*q0 = ±1`.
- The distance from `p1/q1` to `x` is `d/(q1*self._denominator)`, where `d` is the leftover Euclid remainder.
- So `p1/q1` is at least as close exactly when `2*d*(q0+k*q1) <= self._denominator`.

The `<=` sends ties to `p1/q1`, the smaller denominator. The same identity guarantees both candidates are already in lowest terms, which is why `_from_coprime_ints` can skip the gcd.

**Why not just round.** Rounding, as in `round(x * M) / M`, only considers the single denominator `M` (or its divisors after reduction). The best approximation with denominator *at most* `M` usually has some unrelated, smaller denominator:

| Input | Limit | Rounding to that denominator | `limit_denominator` |
|---|---|---|---|
| π ≈ 3.14159… | 10 | 31/10 (error about 0.04) | 22/7 (error about 0.0013) |
| π ≈ 3.14159… | 100 | 314/100 (error about 0.0016) | 311/99 (error about 0.0002) |

To get the right answer by rounding, you would have to round against every denominator from 1 to `M` and keep the best, which is `M` steps. The loop gets there in a number of iterations proportional to the number of digits in `M`, using only exact integer arithmetic.

The second row also shows why the semiconvergent step matters. The convergents of π are 3, 22/7, 333/106, and 333/106 is over the limit. Stopping at 22/7 would be wrong: with `k = (100 - 1)//7 = 14` the semiconvergent is `(3 + 14*22)/(1 + 14*7) = 311/99`, which is closer.

**`firstweekday` and `monthdayscalendar`.** It only changes which weekday sits in column 0; the day numbers themselves are the same. That shifts the zero padding: the first week gets `(day1 - firstweekday) % 7` leading zeros, and the last week is padded with zeros to a full seven. Because the padding moves, the number of rows can change too. February 2021 (28 days, starts on a Monday) is 4 rows with `firstweekday=0` but 5 rows with `firstweekday=6`.

**Edges of the year range.** Yes, there is a surprise: `itermonthdates` has no edge handling at all. It turns every `(y, m, d)` from `itermonthdays3` into a `datetime.date`, including the padding days from the neighbouring months, so at the limits it raises `ValueError` in a way that depends on `firstweekday`:

- **January of year 1:** 1 January 0001 is a Monday, so it works with `firstweekday=0`. Any other setting needs padding days from December of year 0 and fails on the first item.
- **December 9999:** 31 December 9999 is a Friday, so it only works cleanly with `firstweekday=5` (weeks starting Saturday). Otherwise it yields all of December and then fails on the first padding day in January 10000.

Because it is a generator, the December failure arrives mid-iteration, after valid dates have already been yielded. `monthdatescalendar` and `yeardatescalendar` call `list()` on it, so they simply fail outright.

The other iterators do not have this problem. `weekday()` maps out-of-range years onto `2000 + year % 400`, so `itermonthdays`, `itermonthdays2`, `itermonthdays3`, `itermonthdays4` and `monthdayscalendar` work for year 0 or year 10000 and beyond. That is what the "can be used for dates outside of datetime.date range" note in the `itermonthdays3` docstring is pointing at.

`budget.py` now takes an optional month: `python3 budget.py 2026-09` counts only September's transactions, and with no argument it prints exactly what it did before. I ran it both ways against your data:

| Envelope | No month (all transactions) | `2026-09` |
|---|---|---|
| groceries | 174.60 | 371.55 |
| fuel | 22.85 | 124.75 |
| eating out | 45.75 | 84.25 |
| household | 54.61 | 101.60 |

- **Bad input:** a month that isn't `YYYY-MM` (for example `sept` or `2026-13`), or more than one argument, prints a short error and exits with status 2.
- **Empty months:** a month with no transactions shows every envelope at its full allocation rather than an error.
